title: Living Creatures: Exploring Their Characteristics
description: Grade 6 Science: the characteristics of living organisms (growth, respiration, response to stimuli and more) and an introduction to vertebrates and invertebrates.

topics.title: Characteristics of Living Organisms
topics.concept:
How do we know whether something is living or non-living? A car can move and a river can flow, yet neither is alive; a seed lies still, yet it is living. We decide by checking for a set of features that all living things share, called the characteristics of living organisms. A thing is living if it shows these life processes:

  • Growth — living things grow in size, increasing from within. A seed grows into a plant; a kitten grows into a cat.
  • Need for food (nutrition) — living things need food for energy and growth. Plants make their own food; animals take in food.
  • Respiration — living things breathe; they take in air and use the oxygen in it to release energy from food.
  • Response to stimuli — living things react to changes around them. A change that causes a reaction is a stimulus. We pull our hand away from a hot object; a plant bends towards light; a touch-me-not (Mimosa) folds its leaves when touched.
  • Movement — living things move on their own. Animals move from place to place; plants show slower movements, such as roots growing down and shoots growing up.
  • Excretion — living things get rid of the waste their bodies make.
  • Reproduction — living things produce more of their own kind (young ones, eggs or seeds).

Living things show all these features; a non-living thing may show one (a car moves) but not the others. Finally, all living things have a definite life span — they are born, grow, and one day die.

examples.problem: Example 1: A car can move and uses fuel, yet it is non-living. Give two reasons why.
examples.solution:
Living things must show all the life processes, not just one.

  • A car cannot grow on its own.
  • It cannot reproduce (make young cars) or respond to stimuli by itself.
examples.answer: A car cannot grow by itself and cannot reproduce or respond to stimuli; movement alone does not make it living.

examples.problem: Example 2: What is a stimulus? Give one example of how a plant responds to one.
examples.solution:
A stimulus is a change that causes a reaction.

  • A stimulus is a change in the surroundings that a living thing reacts to.
  • Example: a plant bends/grows towards light (light is the stimulus).
examples.answer: A stimulus is a change in the surroundings that causes a response; for example, a plant bends towards light.

examples.problem: Example 3: Name the life process by which living things produce more of their own kind.
examples.solution:
Recall the characteristic that continues a species.

  • Producing young ones, eggs or seeds is reproduction.

recap:
• Living things share characteristics: growth, nutrition, respiration, response to stimuli, movement, excretion and reproduction.
  • A stimulus is a change that a living thing reacts to (light, touch, heat).
  • Non-living things may show one feature (a car moves) but not all.
  • All living things have a definite life span — they are born, grow and die.

quiz.q: Which of these is a characteristic of all living things?
quiz.explanation: All living things grow and reproduce, among other life processes.

quiz.q: A change in the surroundings that a living thing reacts to is called a:
quiz.explanation: A stimulus is a change that causes a response.

topics.title: Vertebrates and Invertebrates
topics.concept:
The animal world is huge and varied. To study animals, scientists divide them into groups. One of the most useful divisions is based on the backbone — the row of small bones (the spine) running down the middle of the back. Animals are grouped as:

  • Vertebrates — animals that have a backbone. They usually have a well-developed skeleton inside the body. Examples: fish, frog, snake, sparrow, cat, human.
  • Invertebrates — animals that do not have a backbone. Examples: ant, butterfly, spider, earthworm, snail, jellyfish. Most animals on Earth are actually invertebrates.

Vertebrates themselves are divided into five well-known groups, each with its own features:

  • Fish — live in water, breathe with gills, have fins and a body covered with scales.
  • Amphibians — such as frogs; can live both in water and on land.
  • Reptiles — such as snakes and lizards; crawl and have dry, scaly skin.
  • Birds — have feathers, wings and a beak; most can fly.
  • Mammals — such as cats, cows and humans; usually have hair on the body and feed their young on milk.

Grouping animals like this helps us see how they are similar and different, and makes the great variety of animal life easier to study and understand.

examples.problem: Example 1: Classify as vertebrate or invertebrate: sparrow, ant, snake, snail.
examples.solution:
Check each for a backbone.

  • Sparrow and snake have a backbone → vertebrates.
  • Ant and snail have no backbone → invertebrates.
examples.answer: Sparrow and snake are vertebrates; ant and snail are invertebrates.

examples.problem: Example 2: To which group of vertebrates does an animal with feathers, wings and a beak belong?
examples.solution:
Match the features to the group.

  • Feathers, wings and a beak are the features of birds.
examples.answer: It belongs to the group of birds.

examples.problem: Example 3: Why is the presence of a backbone a useful feature for grouping animals?
examples.solution:
A clear, common feature makes a good basis for grouping.

  • Every animal either has a backbone or does not — a clear yes/no.
  • So it neatly divides all animals into two big groups for easy study.
examples.answer: Because every animal either has a backbone or not, it cleanly divides all animals into two groups, making them easier to study.

recap:
• Animals are grouped by the backbone: vertebrates (with backbone) and invertebrates (without).
  • Examples — vertebrates: fish, frog, snake, bird, human; invertebrates: ant, spider, earthworm, snail.
  • Vertebrates form five groups: fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals.
  • Most animals on Earth are invertebrates.

quiz.q: Animals that do NOT have a backbone are called:
quiz.explanation: Invertebrates are animals without a backbone.

quiz.q: A frog, which can live both in water and on land, belongs to which group of vertebrates?
quiz.explanation: Amphibians, such as frogs, can live both in water and on land.

questions.q: Which of these is a characteristic of all living things?
questions.explanation: Living things grow, respire, reproduce and show other life processes.

questions.q: The increase in size of a living thing from within is called:
questions.explanation: Living things grow in size from within.

questions.q: Taking in air and using oxygen to release energy from food is called:
questions.explanation: Respiration releases energy from food using oxygen.

questions.q: A change in the surroundings that causes a living thing to react is a:
questions.explanation: A stimulus is a change that causes a response.

questions.q: A touch-me-not plant folds its leaves when touched. The touch is a:
questions.explanation: The touch is the stimulus; folding the leaves is the response.

questions.q: Getting rid of the waste made by the body is called:
questions.explanation: Removing body waste is excretion.

questions.q: Producing more of one's own kind is called:
questions.explanation: Reproduction produces young ones, eggs or seeds.

questions.q: A car can move but is non-living because it cannot:
options: Grow and reproduce on its own
questions.explanation: A car cannot grow or reproduce by itself, so it is non-living.

questions.q: Animals that HAVE a backbone are called:
questions.explanation: Vertebrates are animals with a backbone.

questions.q: Which of these is an invertebrate?
questions.explanation: An earthworm has no backbone, so it is an invertebrate.

questions.q: Fish breathe in water using their:
questions.explanation: Fish use gills to breathe in water.

questions.q: Animals with feathers, wings and a beak belong to the group of:
questions.explanation: Birds have feathers, wings and a beak.

questions.q: Cats, cows and humans, which feed their young on milk, are:
questions.explanation: Mammals usually have hair and feed their young on milk.

questions.q: An animal that can live both in water and on land, like a frog, is a/an:
questions.explanation: Amphibians, such as frogs, live both in water and on land.

questions.q: All living things finally have a definite:
options: Life span (they are born, grow and die)
questions.explanation: Every living thing has a life span: it is born, grows and dies.

questions.q: A seed lies still and does not move, yet it is living because it can:
questions.explanation: A seed holds life and can grow into a new plant, a key sign of being living.

questions.q: A river flows and a flame flickers, but both are non-living because they cannot:
questions.explanation: Movement alone is not life; non-living things cannot grow, feed or reproduce.

questions.q: A spider, a snail and a jellyfish are placed in the SAME group because they all:
questions.explanation: All three are invertebrates — they have no backbone.

questions.q: Pulling your hand away quickly from a hot pan shows the life process of:
questions.explanation: Reacting to the heat (a stimulus) is response to stimuli.

questions.q: Which feature is shared by a sparrow and a bat (both can fly), placing the bat among mammals not birds?
options: The bat feeds its young on milk and has hair, not feathers
The bat lays eggs in water
questions.explanation: A bat is a mammal because it has hair and feeds its young milk, even though it flies.

questions.q: Why is grouping animals by the backbone helpful to scientists?
options: It cleanly splits all animals into two big groups for study
questions.explanation: Every animal either has a backbone or not, so this gives two clear groups that make study easier.
